title: "Category 2  Self-supervised representation learning for time series"
description: "Learning representations from unlabelled sensor, health and energy data"
toc: true
toc-depth: 2

<span id="top"></span>

A **time series** is an ordered sequence of measurements. A wearable device may record acceleration every fraction of a second, an ECG contains voltage measurements from several leads, and an industrial plant records pressure, flow, temperature and energy over time. These signals contain repeated patterns, trends and operating phases, but useful labels—such as a person's activity, a diagnosis or an abnormal production cycle—may require expert work and are often scarce.

**Self-supervised learning (SSL)** learns from the unlabelled recordings by creating its own training task. A model might make two valid views of the same signal agree, hide part of a sequence and predict it, or predict the representation of a future segment. The resulting encoder converts a recording or window into a compact numerical representation. A small classification or regression head is then trained for a downstream task.

The important question is not whether the pretraining loss decreases, but whether the learned representation reduces the amount of labelled data needed and transfers to new people, machines or operating conditions. Every project therefore compares SSL with a fully supervised model and a randomly initialised encoder on leakage-safe splits.

::: {.category-callout}
**Three ideas to understand**

Contrastive learning aligns valid views of the same recording. Masked modelling reconstructs hidden samples or patches. Latent prediction estimates hidden representations instead of raw values and requires explicit collapse monitoring. Possible MSc contributions include view or mask designs based on the physics or physiology of the signal.
:::

## Learn first and find ideas

- Methods with code: [TS-TCC](https://github.com/emadeldeen24/TS-TCC), [TS2Vec](https://github.com/zhihanyue/ts2vec), [TF-C](https://github.com/mims-harvard/TFC-pretraining) and [SimMTM](https://github.com/thuml/SimMTM).
- Data sources: [UCI Machine Learning Repository](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/), [PhysioNet](https://physionet.org/), [UCR/UEA archive](https://www.timeseriesclassification.com/), [Monash forecasting archive](https://forecastingdata.org/) and [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/).
- Monitor embedding variance and covariance from the first epoch in latent-predictive work. A smooth pretraining loss does not establish that the representation is useful.

## 2.1  Tetra Pak industrial collaboration: Regime-aware self-supervised learning for non-stationary filtration cycles {#project-2-1}

::: {.project-meta}
<span class="meta-label">Task</span><span class="meta-value">Self-supervised multivariate time-series learning, then cycle-level regression or anomaly detection</span>
<span class="meta-label">Level</span><span class="meta-value">MSc only — a BSc route opens only if pre-segmented, regime-labelled data is available before allocation</span>
<span class="meta-label">Compute</span><span class="meta-value">Light to moderate; compact models on a 4–8 GB GPU</span>
<span class="meta-label">Data</span><span class="meta-value">Partner-supplied by Tetra Pak under an approved agreement; not public</span>
<span class="meta-label">Starting paper</span><span class="meta-value">Yue et al., [TS2Vec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.10466), AAAI 2022</span>
:::

::: {.project-intro}
**What you will do.** Membrane-filtration plants generate repeated production and cleaning cycles containing flow, pressure, temperature and energy measurements. Cycle-to-cycle differences are large. You will learn representations that account for the plant's operating regimes, then test whether they predict an operational target better than representations that ignore regime.
:::

**Data.** Tetra Pak provides anonymised process data or an approved secure environment. Requested signals include flow, pressure, temperature, power or energy, setpoints, product/line/phase identifiers, cycle boundaries and available alarms or cleaning records. Expect a few months of roughly minute-level data. Split by complete cycle and preserve time order; overlapping windows are not independent cycles.

**Methods and code.** [TS2Vec](https://github.com/zhihanyue/ts2vec), [TS-TCC](https://github.com/emadeldeen24/TS-TCC) or [SimMTM](https://github.com/thuml/SimMTM), with a compact 1-D CNN, TCN or GRU encoder. Change-point detection, clustering and PCA/UMAP support the initial regime analysis.

**Baselines and evaluation.** Compare a regime-specific statistical baseline, a supervised TCN/GRU, generic SSL across all cycles and a regime-aware or regime-conditioned encoder, with random-frozen and frozen-probe controls. Primary metric is MAE for energy regression or AUPRC for anomaly scoring, reported with label-efficiency budgets and at least three seeds.

::: {.scope .scope-msc}
**Master research question.** **Can cycle-phase- and operating-regime-aware self-supervised views separate legitimate process variation from energy inefficiency or abnormal behaviour better than generic augmentations?** The contribution is the process-aware view or masking design plus a matched-budget comparison against generic augmentation, including transfer to a held-out regime, line or product. Rerunning an unchanged TS2Vec or TS-TCC is a reproduction, not the contribution.
:::

::: {.scope .scope-bsc}
**Why this is not normally a Bachelor project.** Two reasons. Data access is gated by the partner agreement, so the start date cannot be guaranteed. More importantly, identifying the operating regimes is itself an unsupervised problem with no ground truth — a Bachelor student would have to both discover the regimes and use them as the main experimental factor, which makes the result impossible to interpret if the regimes are wrong. A Bachelor route opens only when the regimes can be defined from setpoint, product or line metadata and the cycles are already segmented.
:::

**Practical notes.** Confirm cycle boundaries, units, synchronisation, missingness, regime metadata, independent-cycle count and one defensible target before modelling. Data and trained artefacts remain subject to the AU–Tetra Pak agreement.

## 2.2  Contrastive learning for wearable activity recognition {#project-2-2}

::: {.project-meta}
<span class="meta-label">Task</span><span class="meta-value">Self-supervised time-series representation learning, then classification</span>
<span class="meta-label">Level</span><span class="meta-value">BSc or MSc</span>
<span class="meta-label">Compute</span><span class="meta-value">Light; CPU or 4 GB GPU</span>
<span class="meta-label">Data</span><span class="meta-value">[UCI Human Activity Recognition](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/240/human+activity+recognition+using+smartphones) — 30 subjects, 6 activities, 10,299 windows, 50 Hz, CC BY 4.0</span>
<span class="meta-label">Starting paper</span><span class="meta-value">Eldele et al., [TS-TCC](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.14112), IJCAI 2021</span>
:::

::: {.project-intro}
**What you will do.** A phone records acceleration and angular velocity while a person walks, sits or climbs stairs. Learn an encoder from the unlabelled sensor windows, freeze it, and measure how few labels a small classifier needs to recognise activities.
:::

**Data.** UCI HAR, about 58 MB, with a standard subject-independent split. Preserve subject grouping: never place windows from the same subject in both training and test sets.

**Methods and code.** [TS-TCC](https://github.com/emadeldeen24/TS-TCC) or [TS2Vec](https://github.com/zhihanyue/ts2vec) — choose **one**. Use the same 1-D CNN or small Transformer encoder for the self-supervised and supervised comparisons.

**Baselines and evaluation.** Random frozen encoder, SSL frozen linear probe, SSL fine-tuning and a fully supervised model trained from scratch. Report accuracy and macro-F1 on the subject-independent split.

::: {.scope .scope-bsc}
**Bachelor research question.** **How much labelled activity data can self-supervised pretraining replace?**

*Core experiment.* Produce a full label-efficiency curve at 1%, 5%, 10%, 25% and 100% of the labels, for all four conditions above. At the 1% and 5% budgets, resample **which** labels are used across at least five subject-stratified draws and report confidence intervals — a single 1% sample can come from only one or two subjects, which would make that end of the curve meaningless.

A strong result quantifies a statement such as: *with 10% of the labels, self-supervised pretraining reaches X% of the performance achieved with all labels.*
:::

::: {.scope .scope-msc}
**Master research question.** **Do physics-consistent SO(3) orientation views improve label efficiency and orientation robustness more than signal-agnostic jitter, scaling and permutation?** Separate gravity from body acceleration, rotate the accelerometer and gyroscope triads together as a rigid body would actually move, and ablate each step. This needs no new data collection — the rotations are applied to the existing recordings. The insight comes from physically valid view construction, not from tuning augmentation strength.
:::

## 2.3  Lead-aware masked learning for 12-lead ECG {#project-2-3}

::: {.project-meta}
<span class="meta-label">Task</span><span class="meta-value">Self-supervised multivariate time-series learning, then multi-label classification</span>
<span class="meta-label">Level</span><span class="meta-value">MSc only — a BSc route is possible with a supplied PTB-XL dataloader and shared encoder</span>
<span class="meta-label">Compute</span><span class="meta-value">Moderate; 8 GB GPU recommended</span>
<span class="meta-label">Data</span><span class="meta-value">[PTB-XL](https://physionet.org/content/ptb-xl/1.0.3/) — 21,799 ECGs, 18,869 patients, 100/500 Hz, CC BY 4.0, no credentialing</span>
<span class="meta-label">Starting paper</span><span class="meta-value">Dong et al., [SimMTM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.00861), NeurIPS 2023</span>
:::

::: {.project-intro}
**What you will do.** A 12-lead ECG observes the same cardiac event from different electrical viewpoints. Instead of masking arbitrary time patches, the model hides complete leads or anatomical lead groups and predicts their latent representations from the visible leads.
:::

**Data.** PTB-XL at 100 Hz, using the official patient-aware folds: 1–8 for training, 9 for validation, 10 for testing. The dataset is fully labelled, so label budgets simulate scarcity rather than reflecting missing annotations.

**Methods and code.** [SimMTM](https://github.com/thuml/SimMTM), [TF-C](https://github.com/mims-harvard/TFC-pretraining) or [TS2Vec](https://github.com/zhihanyue/ts2vec), with a 1-D ResNet or compact Transformer as the shared encoder.

**Baselines and evaluation.** Random frozen encoder, frozen probe, fine-tuning and the same encoder fully supervised. Macro-AUROC on fold 10 across the five diagnostic superclasses is the primary endpoint; add macro-AUPRC for class imbalance. Report patient-level splits and several label budgets.

::: {.scope .scope-msc}
**Master research question.** **Can a lead-identity-conditioned predictor reconstruct the latent representation of missing leads without collapse, and does that improve low-label diagnosis?** Develop complete-lead and anatomical-group masking, predictor conditioning and collapse diagnostics, then ablate masking granularity, EMA schedule and predictor depth. This route is methodologically risky: structured masking can collapse, so monitor embedding variance and covariance from the first epoch.
:::

::: {.scope .scope-bsc}
**Bachelor route (only if a PTB-XL dataloader and shared encoder are supplied).** Choose **one** of two questions.

**(a) Contrastive learning or masked modelling: which objective produces better ECG representations?** Implement both objectives on **one identical encoder**. This is essential: comparing two published repositories against each other would confound the objective with the encoder architecture, the augmentation settings and how much each implementation was already tuned, and no conclusion about contrastive versus masked learning could be drawn. Only the pretext task may differ.

**(b) How many ECG leads do you actually need?** Train and evaluate using 12 leads, 6 leads, 3 leads and lead II alone, and measure how diagnostic performance falls as leads are removed. This is directly relevant to single-lead wearable devices, needs one codebase, and establishes which leads carry the diagnostic signal that the Master route then exploits.
:::

## 2.4  Self-supervised forecasting representations for energy series {#project-2-4}

::: {.project-meta}
<span class="meta-label">Task</span><span class="meta-value">Self-supervised time-series learning, then temporal regression</span>
<span class="meta-label">Level</span><span class="meta-value">BSc or MSc</span>
<span class="meta-label">Compute</span><span class="meta-value">Light to moderate; 4–8 GB GPU</span>
<span class="meta-label">Data</span><span class="meta-value">[ETT](https://github.com/zhouhaoyi/ETDataset) — electricity transformer temperature, hourly (ETTh1/ETTh2) and 15-minute (ETTm1/ETTm2) subsets</span>
<span class="meta-label">Starting paper</span><span class="meta-value">Woo et al., [CoST](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.01575), ICLR 2022</span>
:::

::: {.project-intro}
**What you will do.** Pretrain an encoder on one unlabelled energy series, freeze it, and fit a small forecasting head. The core comparison asks whether a reusable representation transfers to a *different* series, or whether a purpose-built supervised forecaster trained directly on that series is simply better.
:::

**Data.** Use ETT with chronological splits, fitting scalers on the training period only. ETTh1 and ETTh2 come from two different transformers, which provides genuine distribution shift; ETTh1 to ETTm1 additionally changes the sampling rate.

**Methods and code.** [CoST](https://github.com/salesforce/CoST), [TS2Vec](https://github.com/zhihanyue/ts2vec) or [SimMTM](https://github.com/thuml/SimMTM) for pretraining. [DLinear](https://github.com/cure-lab/LTSF-Linear) is the required supervised reference; [PatchTST](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.14730) is optional. A ridge or linear head on frozen representations is the key diagnostic.

**Baselines and evaluation.** Seasonal-naive, DLinear, frozen SSL representation with a ridge head, and SSL fine-tuning. Report MSE and MAE at agreed horizons with identical input lengths and chronological splits, plus three seeds.

::: {.scope .scope-bsc}
**Bachelor research question.** **Do self-supervised representations pretrained on one energy series transfer to a different one?**

*Core experiment.* Pretrain the encoder once on ETTh1, then probe and fine-tune it on ETTh2, comparing against the same encoder pretrained directly on ETTh2 and against DLinear trained on ETTh2. An ETTh1-to-ETTm1 variant additionally tests transfer across sampling rates. Add a second dataset only after the first pipeline is stable.

**Expected outcome.** DLinear is a very strong baseline on ETT and may beat the self-supervised pipeline outright. That is a valid and useful finding for this project — report it and analyse why, rather than tuning until the representation appears to win.
:::

::: {.scope .scope-msc}
**Master research question.** **Do decomposition-aligned positive pairs improve transfer and low-data forecasting when seasonal phase drifts?** Use a stable period or seasonal decomposition to select positives, compare with random cropping and frequency-domain contrast, and analyse failure on non-stationary intervals. A negative result is useful if it identifies when estimated seasonality is unreliable. Period estimation can consume the whole thesis, so validate on clean ETT seasonality first.
:::

## 2.5  Self-supervised learning on heat-pump smart-meter data {#project-2-5}

::: {.project-meta}
<span class="meta-label">Task</span><span class="meta-value">Time-series representation learning, then household-level classification</span>
<span class="meta-label">Level</span><span class="meta-value">MSc only — a BSc route opens once the data licence and label counts are confirmed</span>
<span class="meta-label">Compute</span><span class="meta-value">Light to moderate after preprocessing</span>
<span class="meta-label">Data</span><span class="meta-value">[HEAPO on Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/records/15056919) — 1,408 households; licence must be confirmed before use</span>
<span class="meta-label">Starting paper</span><span class="meta-value">Brudermueller et al., [HEAPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.16993), 2025</span>
:::

::: {.project-intro}
**What you will do.** HEAPO contains a large pool of households with smart-meter data but no inspection labels, and a much smaller pool with both. You will pretrain on the unlabelled households and test whether that improves classification on the small labelled group.
:::

**Data.** The paper reports 214 treatment households with smart-meter data and inspection information, 1,194 control households without labels, and 410 inspection protocols. Use the [official MIT-licensed dataloader](https://github.com/tbrumue/heapo) rather than writing a new pipeline. Group all splits by household.

⚠️ **Licence check required.** The paper is CC BY 4.0, but that does not license the data, and Zenodo's rights metadata does not display a dataset licence. Confirm reuse terms with the depositor before the project starts. Also verify label prevalence and class balance at the same time — see the note below.

**Methods and code.** [TS2Vec](https://github.com/zhihanyue/ts2vec), [TS-TCC](https://github.com/emadeldeen24/TS-TCC) or a masked model such as [SimMTM](https://github.com/thuml/SimMTM), with a 1-D CNN, InceptionTime or LSTM as the supervised comparison. Start from heat-pump type or another sufficiently prevalent label.

**Baselines and evaluation.** Random frozen encoder, frozen SSL probe, SSL fine-tuning and end-to-end supervised training on identical household-grouped splits. Weather-only and metadata-only baselines show what the load series adds. Report balanced accuracy and macro-F1 with confidence intervals.

::: {.scope .scope-msc}
**Master research question.** **Can unlabelled data from a large related household population improve prediction on a much smaller labelled population, and do weather- and cycle-aware views improve it further?** Compare pretraining sources — none, labelled households only, unlabelled control households, and all households — then add outdoor-temperature-matched positives or whole-cycle masking and ablate the weather conditioning.

**A note on statistical power.** There are only 214 labelled households, so a grouped test fold holds roughly 40–70 of them and confidence intervals on accuracy are wide — wider than the improvement self-supervised pretraining typically produces. Use repeated grouped cross-validation, decide the single primary comparison in advance rather than testing all four pretraining sources against each other, and report confidence intervals throughout. A carefully executed study that concludes the difference cannot be resolved at this sample size is a valid outcome for this project.
:::

::: {.scope .scope-bsc}
**Bachelor route (only after the licence is cleared and label counts verified).** Use the official dataloader, pick the single most prevalent and balanced label, and compare just two pretraining sources — none versus unlabelled control households — on household-grouped splits, with a label-efficiency curve. The power note above applies equally.
:::

## 2.6  Graph self-supervised learning from vibration signals {#project-2-6}

::: {.project-meta}
<span class="meta-label">Task</span><span class="meta-value">Graph-level classification (one graph per signal window) with cross-operating-condition transfer</span>
<span class="meta-label">Level</span><span class="meta-value">MSc only</span>
<span class="meta-label">Compute</span><span class="meta-value">Moderate preprocessing; small models on a 4–8 GB GPU</span>
<span class="meta-label">Data</span><span class="meta-value">[Paderborn KAt](https://mb.uni-paderborn.de/en/kat/research/bearing-datacenter/data-sets-and-download) (~5 GB, CC BY-NC 4.0) for the main study; [CWRU](https://engineering.case.edu/bearingdatacenter) for pipeline development</span>
<span class="meta-label">Starting paper</span><span class="meta-value">Wang et al., [graph representation via wavelet packet decomposition with graph contrastive pretraining](https://consensus.app/papers/details/79e279fadf3d57a696aff3fe416c9c7c/), 2025</span>
:::

::: {.project-intro}
**What you will do.** A vibration window has no natural graph — you construct one. Each window becomes its own graph whose **nodes are frequency bands fixed by bearing geometry** and whose **edges measure which of those bands are modulated together in that window**. You pretrain a graph encoder without fault labels, then test whether the representation transfers to operating conditions it never saw during training.
:::

**How the graph is built.** This is the core design decision, so it is specified rather than left open:

1. **Order-domain resampling.** Resample each window from uniform time steps to uniform shaft-angle steps (computed order tracking), so the spectrum axis becomes orders — cycles per shaft revolution — instead of Hz.
2. **Fixed node vocabulary.** Bearing characteristic frequencies scale with shaft speed, but their *ratios* to shaft speed are pure geometry and therefore speed-invariant. Define nodes as order bands centred on BPFO, BPFI, BSF and FTF and their harmonics, plus shaft harmonics and a set of broadband bands — roughly 30–40 nodes. Node *identity* is then the same in every window, at every speed. Give the bands finite width (about ±1.5%) because rolling-element slip shifts real fault components off their theoretical orders.
3. **Node features, per window.** Band energy, envelope-spectrum amplitude at that order, spectral kurtosis, band RMS.
4. **Edges, per window.** A fault produces a periodic impact train that rings several structural resonances at once, so the envelopes of those bands rise and fall together. Measure that with envelope correlation between band-filtered components, or with cyclic spectral coherence. Restrict candidate edges to a physics backbone — harmonics within a fault family, and carrier-to-sideband pairs (BPFI ± shaft order, BSF ± FTF) — then let the window's data set the weights, and keep the top-k per node.

So the node set is fixed across the dataset while **features and edge weights are recomputed for every window** — the co-modulation pattern is the diagnostic signal.

**Data.** Paderborn KAt (32 bearings, four operating conditions, 64 kHz vibration plus recorded speed, torque and radial load) is the main dataset, via the [download page](https://groups.uni-paderborn.de/kat/BearingDataCenter/); its recorded speed makes order tracking straightforward. CWRU is for building the pipeline. Split by **bearing**, never by window.

**Methods and code.** A GIN encoder on the window graphs, pretrained with [GraphCL](https://github.com/Shen-Lab/GraphCL) (contrastive) or [GraphMAE](https://github.com/THUDM/GraphMAE) (masked feature reconstruction) — both are graph-level methods, unlike node-level approaches such as BGRL. Note that the standard GraphCL augmentations need care here: dropping the BPFO 2× node does not perturb the graph, it deletes the evidence.

**Baselines and evaluation.** Two mandatory non-graph baselines: envelope-order-spectrum features with a gradient-boosted classifier, and [cyclic spectral coherence maps with a CNN](https://consensus.app/papers/details/84fff04117ce59238de88bbdf0750b71/) — the established domain method, and the one a graph result has to beat to mean anything. Then a four-arm factorial on identical graphs: physics backbone with per-window weights; the same backbone with weights fixed equal; random edges; and no edges. Accuracy and macro-F1, with **cross-operating-condition transfer as the primary endpoint** — train on one load/speed condition, test on another, with identical held-out conditions for every method. Fit thresholds and normalisation on training data only.

::: {.scope .scope-msc}
**Master research question.** **Does a speed-invariant, kinematics-derived graph representation of a vibration window transfer across operating conditions better than generic time-frequency graphs — and is any gain due to the graph construction, the self-supervised pretraining, or both?**

Existing graph-based bearing diagnosis defines nodes from generic decompositions — wavelet-packet bands or spectrogram bins — which are not comparable across shaft speeds. Defining the node vocabulary from bearing kinematics in the order domain makes the graph structurally invariant to speed, which is what should allow representations to transfer. Testing that is the contribution; GraphCL and GraphMAE are baselines.

**The hypothesis stated sharply.** With a fixed node set you could concatenate every node's features into one vector and run gradient boosting, using all the marginal band information. The graph earns its place only if *which bands co-modulate* carries information the individual band features do not. The four factorial arms test exactly that — and the fixed-weight arm matters most, because if the adjacency were identical for every window the GNN would collapse into a fixed linear operator over node features, which is a structured MLP rather than graph learning.

**Why in-distribution accuracy will not answer this.** CWRU saturates near 99–100% for almost any method, including simple hand-crafted features. If all four arms score within a point of each other, the comparison has resolved nothing. Cross-condition transfer moves performance into a range where the arms can actually be separated.
:::

::: {.scope .scope-bsc}
**Why this is not a Bachelor project.** Before any network is trained, the project requires order tracking, computing fault orders from bearing geometry, slip-tolerant band definition and a defensible edge measure — a substantial block of signal-processing work, and one where the student must justify modelling choices rather than implement a given recipe.
:::

**Related work to start from.** [A 2025 review of GNNs for rolling bearing fault diagnosis](https://consensus.app/papers/details/45287a32d5b25d729adaddd260d62e6b/) maps the field into temporal, feature and spatiotemporal graphs. For the closest existing constructions, see [wavelet-packet bands as nodes with correlation-based edges and graph contrastive pretraining](https://consensus.app/papers/details/44b08e614a825835b47c754b572c692a/), [a GCN over constant-Q spectrogram bins with fundamental-to-harmonic edges](https://consensus.app/papers/details/32c09569a1d85ad9b615a0257fe03331/), and [a physics-informed GCN deriving edge weights from bearing dynamics](https://consensus.app/papers/details/c448358b3db75834bd8e79bf358887b2/). [A graph-level representation-learning paper](https://consensus.app/papers/details/297569cdecb653d98a3c1339eadc85b2/) argues against the more common sample-as-node paradigm. For the signal processing, see [a review of diagnosis under time-varying speeds](https://consensus.app/papers/details/003e7751a57d5dc79488ef5afba983dd/) and [Abboud et al. on envelope analysis in variable-speed conditions](https://consensus.app/papers/details/e434edd6bd8055fea8233cc9b94879fc/).
